```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(knbsdata)
```

The KNBS census data service publishes tables from the 2019 Kenya Population
and Housing Census — population, health, ICT and household characteristics —
through a machine-readable API, under an explicit **CC BY 4.0** licence
statement. `knbs_indicators()` lists those tables and `knbs_get_indicator()`
returns one as tidy observations.

Chunks that contact the service are shown but not run, so building this
vignette never depends on it.

## What this source is, and is not

Three properties worth knowing before you use it:

- **It is census data.** Every table describes 2019. There are no time series
  here: `period` is 2019 throughout, and `frequency` is `NA` because a census
  table is not a recurring release. Consumer prices, GDP and other running
  indicators are *not* in this source (see the source-status vignette for
  where that work stands).
- **It is served over plain HTTP.** The API host has no TLS listener, so
  traffic to it is unencrypted in transit. It carries only public census
  aggregates and no credentials; the registry records the exception
  explicitly.
- **It is first-party.** The service is operated by KNBS (built with Istat,
  Italy's national statistical institute) and linked from KNBS's own portals
  page.

## Finding a table

```{r, eval = FALSE}
knbs_indicators()
knbs_indicators(topic = "Population")
knbs_indicators(search = "marital")
```

Thirty-two tables across four populated themes at the time of writing.

## Getting observations

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pop <- knbs_get_indicator("POPCEN0001")
pop
```

You can pass a name instead of an id; if several tables match you get an error
listing the candidates rather than a silently chosen one.

The result has one row per cell:

- **Core columns:** `indicator_id`, `indicator_name`, `period`, `value`.
- **Geography**, where the table has it: `geo_code`, `geo_name`, `geo_level`.
  Codes keep their leading zeros — `"00"` is Kenya, two digits are counties,
  four digits are sub-counties — and `geo_level` says which
  (`"national"`, `"county"`, `"subcounty"`).
- **Sex**, where the table has it, using the source's own categories
  (the 2019 census enumerated intersex as well as female and male).
- **Every other dimension** keeps its source id: a code column named for the
  dimension (for example `p18_vs1`) and a matching `<id>_label` column
  ("Marital Status"). The dimension names are in
  `knbs_metadata(pop)$notes`.

## Filtering geography

```{r, eval = FALSE}
counties <- knbs_get_indicator("POPCEN0001", geo_level = "county")
nairobi  <- knbs_get_indicator("POPCEN0001", geo_code = "47")
```

Filters are applied after retrieval — the API serves whole tables — so the
first call and the second cost the same request. Tables are cached for seven
days by default.

## A worked example

County population aged 12+, both sexes, all marital statuses:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
pop <- knbs_get_indicator("POPCEN0001", geo_level = "county")
totals <- pop[pop$sex == "total" & pop$p18_vs1 == "T",
              c("geo_code", "geo_name", "value")]
totals[order(-totals$value), ]
```

Because `geo_code` is character with leading zeros intact, these codes join
cleanly against any other dataset keyed the same way.

## Provenance and citation

```{r, eval = FALSE}
knbs_metadata(pop)
knbs_cite(pop)
```

The metadata carry the licence statement, the release date (`2019-12-31`), the
source statement ("KNBS Population Census 2019") and the dimension list; the
citation is built from them.

## Honesty notes

- `unit` is `NA` in the catalogue: the source does not state units, and
  counts-versus-proportions is knowable only from each table's name. The
  package does not guess.
- An unknown table id is reported as *not found*. (The API itself answers
  those requests with HTTP 200 and a body reading `errore`; the package
  translates.)
- The service checks the *shape* of everything it parses. If the API changes,
  you get `knbs_error_schema_changed`, not a plausible-looking wrong table.
